Conditional mean models, which are widely used in various applications, rely on time-invariant parameters to predict outcomes based on historical data. However, the effectiveness of these models can be impaired by dynamic patterns, such as changing trends and periods, that are common in real-world scenarios. This limitation can result in suboptimal predictions and inaccurate feature learning. To address this challenge, we propose a novel Poisson Autoregressive (PAR) model that incorporates temporal awareness and adaptive learning. Unlike traditional PAR models that use exponential weights, our approach utilizes a combination of long short-term memory (LSTM) and a global renewal theory-based technique, enabling the model to effectively capture and adapt to non-stationary patterns. We also introduce a new technique for modeling time-varying periods, represented by dynamic curves that leverage LSTM outputs. The effectiveness of our proposed model is demonstrated through simulations and real-world applications, including forecasting in ecology and market analysis. The results show that our model effectively captures non-stationary characteristics and outperforms conventional PAR models and LSTM-based approaches. The code for the proposed model is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/lingeling/TDPAR. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct approaches and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through clustering based on those cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining projection clustering and correspondence learning between 2D-3D projections. Specifically, a novel network architecture is proposed that generates two sets of 2D-3D correspondences from both the projected 2D object and 3D model. The first cluster is identified from one set of correspondences, enabling the solution of the Absolute Pose Representation (APR) problem. The learning process is trained end-to-end using the correspondences clustering loss, APR loss, and a adversarial loss to enhance the purity of clusters. The proposed framework along with the 2D-3D projection architecture serves as a powerful tool for pose estimation challenged by occlusion, category-level scenarios. Experimental results indicate the superiority of the proposed framework over existing literature across multiple datasets. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate, interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. This results in a complex calculation that can be computationally demanding, however it offers a versatile tool for various applications, as demonstrated by our examples. This new method provides a solid foundation for further network centrality developments and offers potential uses in network evaluation, resource allocation, and spreading simulations. In addition, we have made available a user-friendly Python implementation of our method called Multicent. It allows for the easy exploration and visualization of multi-layer networks, along with interactive parameter adjustments and results visualization. Our approach and Python implementation can be found at https://github.com/our-group-name/Multicent. Our method has been put to the test on both artificial and real-world networks, including academic collaboration networks, financial transactions, and an internet topology network. These networks have been selected for their diverse characteristics and complexity. Our results show that our method produces meaningful and varied outcomes, as demonstrated by case studies presented in our appendix. These case studies involve the detection of influential nodes, network evaluation, and resource allocation, among other applications. Our new method offers a level of complexity that requires further simplification, however it has the potential to be expanded into a comprehensive multi-layer eigenvector centrality framework. Overcoming this challenge would enable the construction of quantum information systems, but it requires a method to transfer quantum coherence from one system to another, which is difficult to achieve due to the coupling-induced decoherence. Here, we propose a novel quantum-optical catalysis scheme that produces single-photon catalyzed coherent states in a trapped ion system, offering controlled interaction environments and precise detection of the ion's quantum state. Additionally, we provide a quantitative analysis of the conditions necessary to generate photon-number dependent N-photon catalyzed coherent states, and explore the system's ability to generate states that can resist loss and errors, such as catalyzed Glauber states and Fock states. Our proposed scheme has the potential to be adapted for use in various quantum systems, and our results demonstrate that single-photon catalyzed coherent states can be generated under real-world conditions, offering a tangible achievement in overcoming the constraints imposed by classical light sources.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic visualizations. Understanding the electronic and phononic properties of Ta$_2$O$_5$ is crucial due to its applications in photodetectors and energy storage devices. However, its complex chemistry, resulting from competing Ta-O and Ta-Ta interactions, makes its electronic ground state uncertain. To clarify this, we used DFT to simulate its electronic and phononic behavior under different lattice structures, and Monte Carlo methods to accurately calculate the phonon frequencies. Our calculations across various configurations ruled out any Ta-Ta bond existence, instead indicating that Ta forms bonds with oxygen in a distorted Ta$_4$O$_{11}$ lattice. Furthermore, we explored the phonon dispersion and elastic constants for this proposed structure, and found them to be comparable to previously studied Ta$_2$O$_{5-\delta}$ materials. To facilitate experimental verification, we conducted X-ray diffraction simulations and identified any possible lattice structures that could lead to lattice vacancies, in addition to a suspected presence of static disorder along the [100] direction. To complete the understanding, we analyzed the electronic and phononic behavior at both the ab-initio and Monte Carlo levels, revealing any localization of electrons, and the presence of a small frequency of low-damping phonon modes that could be difficult to resolve experimentally. To facilitate further research, we have made our results publicly available, including simulated X-ray diffraction patterns, phonon spectra, and elastic constants for this unique material.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Most existing methods focus on incorporating information from target domains to enhance recommendations in source domains. In contrast, there's a growing need for research on source domain-based suggestions that can benefit target domains. To address this imbalance, we introduce a novel Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation framework called MSDCR. MSDCR explores users' and items' comprehensive aspects to capture their preferences and incorporates them into a multi-branch network. This results in a mechanism that simultaneously learns about the preferences of users and items across multiple domains and provides recommendations based on a balance of intra- and inter-domain preferences. The evaluation of MSDCR using real-world datasets reveals its superiority over baseline methods. Moreover, MSDCR demonstrates its practical applicability by implementing a simple and efficient hyperparameter selection process. MSDCR's effectiveness in addressing multi-sparse-domain sparsity is also validated through a series of controlled experiments. The code for MSDCR is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyangzeng/MSDCR.

The increasing use of magnetic resonance imaging in clinical applications has resulted in a significant number of scans being performed every year. As a consequence, institutions are facing growing challenges in validating the image quality, given their limited resources. This has sparked interest in developing data-driven quality assessment techniques. However, evaluating the performance of such methods poses a problem, especially given that performance assessment itself affects future generalization, creating a loop that makes evaluation more complicated. In addition, institutions with limited data sets face another challenge, including that the models they train may perform well on their own data but may not generalize well to new, unseen scans. We have addressed these challenges in our work by assembling a comprehensive MRI quality assessment dataset consisting of 10 different datasets from various sources, totaling 2,500 scans. We have evaluated several architectures on this combined dataset, testing their performance on separate test sets and comparing them using a novel evaluation method that assesses generalization ability. Our findings have been disclosed in a comprehensive report that also presents previously unpublished images from 13 datasets. We hope this study will serve as a valuable reference for institutions seeking to develop MRI quality assessment generalization capability. We have made our code and the comprehensive MRI quality assessment dataset available to the public.

To mitigate the environmental consequences of transportation, Electric Vehicles (EVs) have gained significant traction in recent years. As a result, there has been an explosion in research related to Charging Infrastructure for EVs. Presently, ownership patterns of privately owned EVs vary greatly between different geographical locations. In this study, a non-linear, non-convex optimization framework is developed to determine the optimal location of EV charging stations, taking into consideration the complex network topology, varying ownership patterns of EVs, and operational constraints of the charging stations. A powerful, efficient solution algorithm has also been devised to address the challenging problem of locating EV charging stations. This solution algorithm is then applied to a real-world scenario in New York City. In this research, a novel framework for creating complex meetings with multiple agents is introduced, focusing on a motivated multi-agent reinforcement learning approach. Each participant's actions are influenced by a controller that considers the current conversation state, aiming to drive the discussion towards a desired outcome. A separate learning loop for each agent optimizes their part in the meeting, while the conversation is controlled by the drive-based motivation. Empirical results show that this motivated learning leads to better meeting outcomes compared to traditional approaches, and demonstrates practical applications in creating interactive storytelling and management scenarios. Recently, a novel ternary compound, GdSn3, with an orthorhombic Cr2Mi3 structure has been discovered, however very little information is available about its electronic and magnetic properties. In this study, the structural, electronic, magnetic properties of GdSn3, CmSn3 and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 were examined using the generalized gradient approximation + on-site Coulomb repulsion (GGA+U) method. It was found that CmSn3 possesses a primitive tetragonal CaBe2 structure and an antiferromagnetic ground state, whereas GdSn3 and the GdxCm1-xSn3 series exhibit the Cr2Mi3 structure with an antiferromagnetic ground state. A comparison of the electronic bands of the two structures revealed a metal-to-semiconductor transition in the series, accompanied by an energy gap of approximately 1.19 eV in the CmSn3 compound. The calculation results were also compared with available experimental data, showing they are in close agreement, albeit with some discrepancies possibly caused by sample temperature variations. The predicted magnetic moments of the GdxCm1-xSn3 series exhibit a linear variation with composition, whereas the lattice parameter, magnetic moment, and the energy gap all show sudden changes at the GdCm equimolar point. The calculated results also predict possible ferromagnetic ground states for both GdSn3 and CmSn3 compounds when the on-site Coulomb repulsion is set to a lower value, which could be confirmed by experimental measurements. The compounds investigated in this study exhibit potential for use in spintronic applications, particularly in controlling the magnetic moments and energy gaps. The results obtained can be utilized to design and optimize the properties of these compounds, and the investigation highlights the importance of further studying this family of compounds. The results of this study can be replicated by using the scripts and input files listed in the appendix. Researchers exploited the Pantheon SN Ia dataset to create novel cosmological constraints by accounting for the effects of weak lensing convergence on the observed magnitudes. Given the small impact of lensing, this approach treated the convergence as a small magnification, expanding the cosmological parameter space to enable derivation of cosmological constraints. Utilizing a specially designed vector technique, a non-parametric approach was taken to create a map of the cosmological parameter space around the standard model. This resulted in a 2D grid of cosmic convergence maps, from which the effects of lensing were subtracted to create a reliable estimate of the SN Ia absolute magnitude dispersion. Converting this magnitude dispersion into a useful cosmological quantity proved straightforward, yielding a convergence fraction of 0.0265 ± 2.2 and a matter density of 0.295 ± 0.13, which are consistent with existing values but less precise due to the limited effect of lensing on SN Ia distances. This indicates that a significantly more precise convergence fraction measurement would be necessary to significantly improve the precision of the matter density measurement, which is currently limited by other errors. Research on silicon-on-insulator (SOI) materials, specifically their photonic versions, holds great promise in accelerating quantum computations by creating a vast amount of qubits. While initial studies have focused on embedding qubits within the core of SOI materials, a novel application involves incorporating qubits in the TET (T-type or trench type, also referred to as T nodes in this context) etched regions. Despite the etched structure providing better confinement and offering a larger quantity of qubit resources, there is limited scientific knowledge about TET structures. This paper aims to explore the fundamental characteristics of TET etched silicon, specifically examining the material's optical properties and etching requirements. By analyzing the optical responses of TET structures with different sizes, we have identified the optimal parameters that yield a particular desired feature - a small gap between the optical resonance. In addition, we have established a clear relationship between the material's optical response and its spatial characteristics. In its current or modified form, this theoretical understanding is applicable to various TET etched silicon structures, facilitating better understanding and more effective implementation of TET etched silicon as quantum anchor nodes. In particular, we have a specific proposal involving a particular TET etched silicon structure - consisting of a double-well structure with a thin middle wall - that offers a substantial quantity of quantum resources at a relatively minimal expense. In our analysis, we have also obtained valuable practical insights that can be applied to this and similar TET etched silicon structures, suggesting that by adjusting the material's depth, it is possible to create a specific optical response that is invariant to the etched node's size. This discovery provides both theoretical and experimental evidence that TET etched silicon structures possess a unique property called size-invariance, which can be influenced by the material's composition and offers considerable advantages in maintaining the consistency of quantum information. Different object detectors exploit scene context for recognition in varying ways.
This work categorizes and evaluates popular deep object detectors with consideration
of scene context, covering 9 leading methods. Context is assessed through both
human evaluations and a more systematic approach using the MS COCO metric.

called the Context Assessment Score (CAS) is presented, offering a numerical
assessment of the context for each detector. On average, our results show that
context-assigned scores reveal a 5 to 10 percent difference in rankings compared
to random context assignments. Additionally, CAS demonstrates practical utility
in selecting an appropriate object detector based on context for a given image,

A key challenge in modern organ transplantation is efficiently managing a limited pool of available kidneys. One-stage and two-stage matching frameworks have been proposed to address this issue, focusing on maximizing the number of transplants. However, these approaches overlook another crucial aspect, which is selecting the most suitable recipients for each donor. In our research, we investigate one-stage and two-stage frameworks where donors can choose the best match from a pool of recipients. For the simplest case with one donor and one recipient type, we establish baseline results using linear programming and chance-constrained methods. More complex scenarios with multiple donors, recipients, and allocation constraints are tackled using a two-stage adaptive algorithm. Our analytical and computational findings demonstrate that considering recipient types and allowing for kidney acceptance/decline decisions by donors can increase the number of transplants by up to 25%. This study was conducted in collaboration with UNOS: the United Network of Organ Sharing. Our research provides optimal and near-optimal solutions for selecting the best match kidney for each donor, which can be valuable for transplant centers looking to optimize their kidney allocation. Our data and algorithm are currently being utilized by UNOS. The most complicated scenarios solved so far involve 3 donor types and 4 recipient types. Our research can be adapted to other organ transplantation applications. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years, spanning 2003 to 2015. During this investigation, we discovered specific issues with previous approaches to evaluating the quality of word2vec, including the frequentist synonyms' distribution, and we propose alternative methods using distributional learning objectives and learning theory. We also leverage financial sentiment labels introduced by Loughran and McDonald (2011) to explore the sectoral-based classification of companies' communication styles, revealing a complex, dynamic structure that we find difficult to anticipate solely using the word2vec model. In fact, we find that word2vec overestimates the importance of frequentist synonyms and neglects entity-based relationships, which are essential for capturing the modularity of companies' communication styles. Our study highlights the limitations of the word2vec model, the challenges of interpreting NLP embeddings, and the risks of misapplication, as well as the potential for our analytical approach to provide a more accurate understanding of the corpora from which these embeddings are derived. We believe that our findings have broader implications for the use of NLP embeddings across various domains. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghassab/word2vec-limitations. Our analysis has been mathematically laid out in the appendix of our related paper titled: The Challenges of Interpreting the Financial Word2Vec Embeddings: The Risk of Misapplication.

In complex systems involving multiple interacting elements, it's often difficult to understand how the interaction affects the equilibrium state, which is the stable state that the system tends to return to. This problem is particularly noticeable in games, where players' individual motivations can result in undesirable group outcomes. To address this challenge, we introduce a new framework that combines deep learning with optimization techniques to make the equilibrium state more understandable by assigning meaningful values to game features, which are represented by a rich and complex set of data. We show that our approach can make the equilibrium state more predictable, as well as more understandable, by using real-world examples such as strategic advertising. We also provide a detailed analysis of our method's strengths and weaknesses along with possible areas for improvement. Our research highlights the potential benefits and challenges of making high-dimensional games more transparent and sheds new light on the study of equilibrium states and their stability. Our code is available at https://github.com/nyg/exgame.

Integrating PDF fitting with theoretical frameworks, especially those that incorporate multiple processes and corrections, is a complex task. For the PDF fitting community, accessing accurate, experimentally verified predictions relies on incorporating these comprehensive frameworks into PDF fitting tools. A proposed theory framework, built using the Drell-Yan process as a test case, aims to provide an adaptable structure for researchers to easily incorporate new processes and inputs. This framework is compatible with widely used PDF fitting tools like APFEL, QCDNUM, and VPDF, and incorporates processes in a way that allows for multiple processes to be treated as sources of systematic uncertainty. Verifying the framework's validity, process-by-process analysis has shown that it accurately replicates the underlying dynamics, and this theory framework is available for other processes and other processes' inputs. Further development of this framework is needed to make it a fully autonomous PDF fitting tool. Until then, it can be accessed in its current form at github.com/theory-group-0/TheoryPDF.

maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a

incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation

automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions. Our approach to this problem of planned 
persuasion incorporates a counterfactual reasoning element, allowing us to 
benchmark against human conversational partners in a controlled setting, where 
conversations are guided by predefined objectives. Our findings, obtained through 
experiments with human partners, demonstrate our ability to engage in diverse 
conversations, accurately determining the degree of understanding between two 
people. Our research, alongside the vast MultiTalk Dataset, is our most

problem of planned persuasion, are our answer to the ongoing challenge of 
creating truly intelligent artificial conversational agents. We outline numerous 
possible approaches to tackle these challenges, concluding with the promise of

The research also takes into consideration the energy dissipation resulting from turbulent fluctuations causing surface curvatures. The near-field volume includes regions where reaction occurs and surface undulations can cause roll-up and vortex formation. The study utilizes a linearized framework to map the reaction of near-field fluctuations to acoustic and hydrodynamic disturbances, while also examining the response of the flame to forcing at different frequencies. Understanding how the functional elements of a genome influence specific traits has been a major challenge in genetics. Researchers have accomplished this by conducting genome-wide association studies, yet the majority of associated genomic sites lack a clear link to trait mechanisms. A comprehensive analysis was performed on 18 human traits involving 88,281 individuals, incorporating data from comprehensive genomic profiling, including gene expression, epigenetic markings, and mutations. The investigation identified specific impacts of genomic alterations on trait mechanisms in all but one of the studied traits, with an average of 58% of associated sites exhibiting a direct effect. Notable examples are highlighted, demonstrating how changes in gene expression, due to modified epigenetic markings or mutations, influence traits, such as height, obesity, hemoglobin levels, cholesterol, blood pressure, fibrinogen levels, kidney stone disease, gastrointestinal diseases, inflammatory responses, stomach cancer, skin melanoma, keratoconus, miscarriages, spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, miscarriage-related pregnancy complications, and coronary artery disease. Furthermore, areas of improvement are discussed, including interindividual variation in trait response to genomic alterations, potential biases in current data sources, limitations in comprehensive genomic profiling, and the complex nature of trait mechanisms. Despite these limitations, this analysis demonstrates the value of integrating genome-wide association studies with comprehensive genomic profiling, offering a deeper understanding of trait mechanisms and refining risk prediction models. The associated database is available at www.genomevariation.org. The findings of this study are relevant to ongoing efforts in genetics research, clinical applications, and personalized medicine. When creating neural conversational agents, we face a significant challenge: determining the variety of semantic labels our model should be exposed to during training. Current approaches largely focus on simple label distributions or prioritize engaging the model in nuanced linguistic tasks like Natural Language Inference. In this work, we explore a more nuanced strategy, varying the semantic labels based on specific dialogue contexts, which we believe is crucial for creating a seamless and natural-language understanding dialogue system. To support this claim, we design a structured communication protocol between the system and user, tailored to evaluate this approach and illustrate the benefits of semantic variety in context. This new composition differs from the original by swapping factors, as seen in the diagram below:
  X ∘ Y = (X ⊗ Y) → (X ⊗ X ⊗ Y ⊗ Y) → (X ⊗ Y ⊗ Y ⊗ X)
Within the based classical monoidal category, this composition is equivalent to the original, yet this property is lost after moving to the disentangled context. By examining the relationship between left and right composites, we find that they become distinct due to the absence of a certain cancellation property. Similarly, the disentangled context can also be applied to classical monoidal categories, yielding a more refined structure. Additionally, we establish that the disentangled category enjoys a more intricate structure, defined by a set of operations that form a braided closed category, which can be further specialized to a symmetric closed category, equivalent to the original classical monoidal category. Lastly, we provide an executable Coq proof verifying this relationship. FedLearn has gained significant popularity for training models on sensitive data across multiple organizations. While focusing on privacy, FedLearn typically employs secure multi-party computation or hardware-based solutions to counter data breaches, yet its efficacy is dependent on competing factors including data size, model complexity, and participant reliability. This paper exposes two concealed threats to vertical FL, which we call Privacy Stealing and Fake Learning. These attacks can be executed independently or in combination, allowing an untrustworthy participant to obtain valuable information from a sensitive dataset with the guise of legitimate model training. We offer a solution to determine the degree of information revealed due to data breaches, which helps evaluate the privacy consequences and provide guidelines for conducting these attacks. We also examine the practical execution of these attacks on real datasets, demonstrating the potential for a malicious participant to conceal a serious security breach while still training a reliable model. Ultimately, we advise researchers and practitioners to exercise caution when selecting participants for FedLearn, citing two concrete examples, including collaboration between competing businesses and between a government agency and private companies. We propose a novel approach called Differentially Private Fake Learning, which adds noise to the model updates instead of the input data, providing a solution to counter similar attacks. We open-source our code and datasets used in this research, which includes real-world datasets obtained from online marketplaces, employee records within a company, and customer information from a banking institution. We estimate the additional computational burden of this approach, which we call the Privacy Cost, which depends on the degree of privacy desired, data size, model complexity, and participant reliability. We examine the trade-off between this cost and the information revealed due to data breaches, which allows for a proper balance between security and efficiency. We further explore the possibility of transferring trained models, which we call Model Stealing, demonstrating that a malicious participant can train a new model on a reduced dataset while still obtaining comparable results to the original model, which allows for an appropriate adjustment of the challenge difficulty. We propose a related challenge called Model Reconstructing, which involves training a model on a hidden label, which allows us to examine the practical execution of this challenge on real datasets, demonstrating the potential for a malicious participant to conceal a serious security breach while still training a reliable model. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Additionally, our approach demonstrates robustness in face reconstruction and manipulation applications. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/zhengyangzhang/SADRNet.

Researchers who utilize silicon donor spin have reached a record for coherence time and one-qubit gate accuracy. To advance further, understanding and controlling spin-spin interaction caused by proximity of donor qubits is crucial. To facilitate this, a computational tool has been developed to simulate the behavior of up to ten donors with long-range interaction in a wide range of conditions. This simulation platform takes into account the precise crystal structure and multiple valley effects in silicon and uses a comprehensive approach that incorporates exchange interactions, Coulomb interactions with lattice, and phonon-induced decoherence. It enables exploration of various configurations, allows for efficient determination of eigenstates and time-evolution of multiple-qubit systems, and has been validated through comparison with experimental results. This tool provides a means for exploring and predicting static and dynamic qubit properties, as demonstrated by our calculations of ground state configurations, quantum beam interference patterns, and time-dependent perturbations induced by interface roughness. This research is applicable to users of silicon-based quantum processors, including superconducting-quantum interface devices and optical interconnects, and highlights the promise of direct spin measurement in hyper-sensitivity applications. Furthermore, it highlights the challenge of removing spin-spin coupling in silicon donor arrays and the necessity for development of theoretical models that go beyond the Hartree-Fock approach. Lastly, it presents a way to experimentally verify multi-valley theory through measurement of interface roughness effects on donor arrays. To facilitate progress in this field, the simulation software, known as NValve, is being made available to the public. In addition to static and dynamic qubit property calculations, NValve allows for direct simulation of space and time resolution of beam interference patterns with Coulomb interference and allows for comparison with experimental results. It also predicts effects of hyper-sensitivity direct spin measurements and provides a means for validating multi-valley theory through measurement of interface roughness effects. In its current form, NValce can handle up to ten qubits, but it has the potential for further development to handle more qubits. Overall, understanding and controlling spin-spin interaction remains a significant challenge for silicon-based quantum processors, but with the development of NValve, this challenge can be met through proper choice of qubit placement, interface roughness reduction, and direct spin measurement techniques that can validate multi-valley theory and provide a roadmap for further development. Lastly, NValve provides a means for investigating effects of hyper-sensitivity direct spin measurements that can lead to breakthroughs in this field.

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves identifying the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, especially using BERT, have led to significant gains in WSD accuracy by employing a binary classification approach.  However, these models have difficulty incorporating background knowledge from word sense lexicons due to the binary classification method's limitation.  As a result, there is a missed opportunity to draw upon valuable information from these resources.  This paper introduces a novel Context-gloss Network (CGN) that integrates both contextual and gloss information.  Contextual information is derived from a context-gloss pair, which we generate using existing methods.  This context-gloss pair allows the model to learn a representation that incorporates the target word's possible senses.  We further propose a strategy to update the contextual representation using a gloss-driven approach.  This approach leverages the sense-annotated lexicon to guide the model learing high-quality features.  We demonstrate CGN's effectiveness across three datasets and three Senses for Words datasets, showcasing a noticeable accuracy improvement over baseline models.  The code is available at https://github.com/linguisic/CGN.

We define a new concept of surface minimizing in metric spaces with boundary, focusing on homotopy classes and without assuming the absence of boundary minimizers. It is demonstrated that these surfaces can be found within their respective homotopy classes, although they may not necessarily be unique. Additionally, when the boundary is composed of minimizing curves in a specific homotopy class, we establish that there is a surface that is both minimizing and has that particular homotopy class as its boundary. Furthermore, we provide a specific example where the unique minimizing surface exists, which demonstrates that such surfaces can vary significantly and are not always unique. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has a problem of scaling due to excessive computational requirements for evaluating test statistics across multiple generators. To address this challenge, we develop a more efficient method called PPPT by utilizing paired tests and permutations in a structured way. Firstly, we divide the data into smaller sets for training a feature extractor and a classifier, which allows us to work with a reduced dimension. Secondly, we generate synthetic counterparts for our data to create reference distributions for the test statistic. Using one-hot encoding, we find that we can efficiently permute these distributions across the classifiers' dimensions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PPPT across multiple systems including BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT for both small and large language models. When comparing our method to traditional paired-permutation testing, we find that PPPT offers significant improvements in accuracy while significantly reducing the required computational time. Additionally, we show that PPPT can be applied to a broader range of systems with little modification, enabling the efficient validation of pre-trained models. We make our code available at github.com/thu-AILab/NLP-Exact-Paired-Permutation-Testing.

This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs interactions. Initially, we consider the Standard Model as the fundamental theory, then expand upon it using the Power Counting method, with an emphasis on developing accurate methods for computing higher-order EFT contributions to double Higgs production. We achieve this by establishing a precise factorization formula and conducting a comprehensive analysis of subleading contributions in both the $h\to hh$ decay and double Higgs production processes. We calculate the scattering amplitude for these processes, identifying relevant operators and providing an in-depth examination of their impact on $hh$ scattering data. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. We leverage our benchmark to gain insight into various models and our proposed framework, finding that our method successfully preserves spatial coherence and detailed geometric structures, whereas many self-supervised baselines fail in this aspect. Nonetheless, overcoming occlusions remains a significant challenge. Nonetheless, we believe this benchmark and the proposed framework will be beneficial for future research on self-supervised flow estimation. In recent times, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have gained significant traction due to their exceptionally high classification efficiencies. However, artificial neural systems have a major drawback - they are extremely power-hungry and require a vast amount of memory, making them challenging to use for resource-constrained devices such as smart sensors. To overcome this obstacle, we present a novel approach based on a Random Neural Network, which leverages both inter- and intra-neuron variability to achieve both high accuracy and energy efficiency in classification tasks. Unlike traditional RNNs that rely on continuous weight updates, our proposed model Leaps to a completely new subset of connection weights per time step, resulting in an exponentially decreased search space that facilitates efficient computation. Additionally, with only a single postsynaptic operation per time step and without the need for continuous weight updates, our model excels in low-power consumption. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our model, we conducted a series of experiments on both spiking and non-spiking versions, which showed our model delivers outstanding performance in comparison to conventional artificial neural networks, outperforming them significantly in terms of both accuracy and energy efficiency. Our proposed model also exhibits robustness in dealing with noisy sensors, as shown in a separate experiment. Our model's efficiency, combined with its simplicity and robustness, makes it an ideal solution for a wide range of classification tasks on constrained devices. Lastly, we applied our model to a real-world dataset and successfully classified it with both high accuracy and low power consumption, as expected. Our model's code is available for public use on GitHub at the specified URL. Moreover, we provide a detailed design of a hardware implementation that could further enhance energy efficiency, as well as a proposal for a scheduled protocol that could boost temporal efficiency. Finally, we outline potential future developments and areas of study.

Modern microservices applications comprise diverse, independently developed services that interact via function calls. As a result, these applications are vulnerable to performance issues and security breaches resulting from excessive system call exposure. Existing solutions, such as Google's gVisor, provide a layered isolation framework that enables services to run in a secure environment while making all system calls accessible to all services. However, this approach can lead to call overhead, security conflicts, and an unwieldy permissions matrix. In addition, determining the optimal system call policies for isolated services is a time-consuming and manual process. In this paper, we present Timeloops, a pioneering approach in automatic system call policy learning for containerized microservices. The Timeloops approach learns the system call policies for isolated services through observation of their execution within a gVisor environment. It develops a set of predefined rules based on normal system calls and flags system calls that are considered malicious. In addition, it creates a graphical representation of the services' call relationships and uses it to guide further investigation into any security breaches. We tested Timeloops on real-world applications, including Apache Kafka and Apache EMBEMLD, and our results show that it reduces call overhead, eliminates unnecessary system call exposure, and successfully learns the system call policies for these services. In fact, when tested against benchmarking tools, it demonstrated a performance improvement of ten to a hundred times. Furthermore, it discovered a security breach in one of the tested applications, YSOFT, which it rectified by limiting system call policies. In summary, Timeloops offers an innovative solution to the problems of system call policies in containerized microservices, which includes performance issues, security conflicts, and call exposure. It provides a free download of its source code. In addition, it presented the results of its research at ACM SIGSAC 2022 conference held in Rimini, Italy. In conclusion, Timeloops represents a groundbreaking achievement in autonomous system call policy learning for secure and high-performance system call interactions in containerized microservices applications. In further development, we are enhancing its capabilities to learn policies for services that use shared libraries and to investigate other isolation frameworks. In addition, we are exploring other applications of Timeloops, including its use in learning policies for virtual machines and in discovering security breaches in complex software systems. In addition, we are open to collaborating with interested researchers and developing Timeloops further. In seismic exploration, accurate imaging is crucial, and image interference presents a significant challenge, causing imaging artifacts that lead to failed acquisitions or poor data quality. Currently, most seismic acquisition strategies, including seismic surveys for oil and gas exploration, strictly adhere to conventional imaging principles to minimize data losses. A novel acquisition method called "extended source signal" (ESS) has been explored, but its full potential is awaiting an advanced signal inversion technique that can handle the data losses associated with it. This study focuses on developing a more effective time-domain inversion approach for this promising acquisition method. By applying a hybrid approach that combines Fourier domain residual compensation and iterative signal inversion, we successfully implemented a feasible and efficient acquisition strategy called "sparsely distributed extended source signal" (SDESS). This approach was tested on synthetic and real data, demonstrating its feasibility and potential. In ecosystems where species compete for resources and colonize new areas, a trade-off between competitive ability and dispersal distance can lead to exclusive or coexisting species dynamics. When the system is subject to random disturbances, the competition can take the form of an elector model with noise, which exhibits a complex interplay of selection, migration, and random events. Our research explores this model, with the aim of understanding how disturbances, a competition-dispersal trade-off, and spatial movement interact to affect the distribution of species and their ability to coexist. We have mathematically proven the existence of a stable equilibrium where a native species excludes a foreign one, as well as conditions under which the two species can coexist. A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear migration occurs. While this process is essential for accurately placing neurons within the proper layer, the underlying mechanisms of interkinetic nuclear migration remain unclear. In this study, we utilize high-speed light microscopy and detailed analysis of a retinal neuroepithelium in developing zebrafish to explore interkinetic nuclear migration. Our findings show that this migration behaves as a diffusive process, supported by data from multiple methods including, lap times, nuclear height, and random walk analysis. Additionally, our research reveals that the tight packaging of cell nuclei within the retinal neuroepithelium is maintained by a layer-specific, density-dependent mechanism. Notably, our results also demonstrate that the decision of a nucleus to move upward or downward is random, yet layer-specific density regulates nuclear migration patterns, contributing to the establishment of a stable, layered structure. Our work provides a new understanding of the mechanical properties of neuroepithelial tissues and the governing principles of interkinetic nuclear migration, offering a simple, diffusion-based theory that accurately replicates the migration patterns observed in the developing zebrafish retina. Our research further suggests that a threshold of 50 densely packed nuclei is necessary to establish a stable, layered structure, a finding with which our data agree and that we propose should be tested in other developing neuroepithelial tissues. Our diffusion-based model also facilitates the analysis of spatial migration patterns, nuclear distribution, and layered structure establishment, all of which are crucial elements of neural development. Our study describes a general principle of neural development, providing a foundation for investigating other developing neuroepithelial tissues and offering potential answers to a variety of developmental questions. We introduce a new approach called Retrieval Enhancement for Unsupervised Domain Adaptive Learning (REUDA), which leverages a comparison between the target and source data to facilitate this cross-task adaptation. These representations serve as inputs to a decoder that generates pseudo-target labels, which are then used to refine the original predictions. We also explore a more challenging semi-supervised scenario, providing an intuitive way to fine-tune the model using these pseudo labels. Our proposed method, REUDA, levers the structure of the target data to guide the unsupervised adaptation, resulting in a significant improvement over baseline methods. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, the Chinese government launched a specialized team to combat misinformation. To effectively manage the dissemination of false information, healthcare officials and digital technology experts must have a clear understanding of how rumors spread and influence online behavior. Therefore, this paper proposes an innovative method to examine the impact of online rumors by analyzing user interactions on social media platforms. Furthermore, it provides a mathematical framework to measure the impact of rumors and offers policy recommendations to control their spread. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, it was applied to real data involving COVID-19-related online rumors in China, showing that it can accurately predict the speed of rumor dissemination, identify key transmission periods, and determine the most influential factors in spreading the rumor. Moreover, by applying influence measurement metrics, it was revealed that online rumors often gain momentum due to the activities of a small number of highly influential users who engage in suspicious behavior. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. The use of standard limit theorem results for random walks then allows us to derive the asymptotic distributions desired. The paper also provides an alternative proof of the independence of the first two positions, which was previously established by Hicks. The asymptotic independence of the first three positions is shown to be true, and we obtain the distance between any two of these three locations as $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sqrt{n}$, with a constant of proportionality, as its asymptotic variance. The results obtained can be generalized to random distributions generated according to the first-order Holton-Muller model. The paper also discusses connections with the related results of various other authors. The research was conducted without any external funding. The paper is composed of five sections. The first section introduces the model and provides background information. The second section investigates the asymptotic behavior of the first two positions. The fifth section concludes the paper. Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings. The complex voltage-period dependence seen in one nanowire, along with the unusual period shifts, have no known theoretical counterparts, highlighting the need for further development in theoretical models to fully capture the observed phenomena. The period shifts are found to be directly related to the dc bias current, a relationship that varies significantly between different nanowires, demonstrating the influence of wire properties on the conductance. The occurrence of period shifts during measurements also correlates with the presence of unusual noise patterns, offering another perspective on their cause. The noise patterns and period shifts share some similarities with effects observed in Josephson junctions at very low temperatures and may indicate a transition to a more chaotic regime, also reflected in the distribution of conductance periods. The possibility of relating the behavior to a non-equilibrium state of the nanowires, specifically a self-sustaining oscillation between chaotic and regular motion, is explored and provides a coherent explanation for the noise patterns, period shifts, and the influence of dc bias current. The possibility of oscillations between chaotic and regular motion also offers a potential pathway for investigating non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and thermodynamics through the study of individual nanowires. The distribution of period shifts during measurements can be described by a Lorentzian distribution, indicating that the spatial distribution of the nanowire's properties may influence the dynamics of individual nanowires more significantly than their average properties. The occurrence of noise patterns and period shifts can be interrupted by destroying the superconducting state of the nanowires, providing further insights into the relationship between the behavior and the presence of a certain noise pattern called fission noise. The possible connection between the dynamics of the nanowires and the noise patterns, including fission noise, is explored and the conditions necessary for generating these patterns in other nanowires are outlined.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between respiratory aerosol particle dynamics, ventilation systems, and probability of droplet transmission from infected individuals to contacts. To better understand and quantify this complex phenomenon, we used a mathematical model incorporating both a fully mixed model and a model simulating the physical and biological mechanisms at play. By comparing these two models, we identified instances where the two approaches diverged significantly. Specifically, our analysis highlighted instances where the spread of disease was overestimated when using a fully mixed model, due to its inability to account for the impact of aerosol particles settling on the bus floor, as well as the limited transmission distance between individuals. Furthermore, our study showed that a more accurate prediction of disease transmission could be achieved by focusing on areas immediately surrounding recently coughed-up aerosol particles, rather than averaging the transmission risk across the entire bus. Along with these key findings, our research also provided a set of non-dimensional groups that can be applied to similar confined environments beyond urban buses. To facilitate this, we offered a graphical representation that can be used to predict the outcome of various transmission scenarios just by plotting a pair of non-dimensional factors against each other. Overall, our study's insights and the introduced non-dimensional framework are valuable tools that can be applied to other settings, such as trains, offices, and supermarkets, all with little modification required. Furthermore, our research highlighted the significance of proper ventilation in reducing the transmission risk, as well as the need for more precise models that take into account the velocity and distribution of respiratory aerosol particles, the movement of individuals, and the physical characteristics of the bus. Along with these suggestions, we are presenting the mathematical model used in our analysis, with the aim of it being beneficial for use in other contexts. With the model, we were able to simulate the transmission dynamics of a bus population, with it also allowing for the comparison of different intervention strategies, as well as the exploration of other phenomena, such as the transmission of the SARS-CoV-2 virus in buses used for long-distance intercity travel. Lastly, we are contributing the introduced graphical representation, non-dimensional groups, and the mathematical model itself to the scientific community, with the hope of it being beneficial for other researchers who may be interested. The investigation of spin-orbit interaction (SOI) beyond its local scope is a growing area of interest, especially for controlling magnetic anisotropy and its influence on magnetic properties. To gain a deeper understanding of SOI, a study of the magnetic anisotropy and its dependence on temperature was conducted on a series of Co/Bi multilayers with different thicknesses, focusing on the proximity effect and spin-orbit interaction near the interface. The results show that the magnetic anisotropy and the anisotropy's temperature variation are influenced by the proximity effect and spin-orbit interaction. Furthermore, a comparison of the experimental findings with theoretical simulations, taking into account the interface interaction and the Rashba effect, reveals that the free electron model overestimates the magnitude of the anisotropy's temperature variation. This discrepancy is attributed to the limited number of free electrons available for magnetic anisotropy in the Bi/Co multilayers. This research demonstrates the importance of considering the limited number of free electrons in calculations of magnetic anisotropy and its temperature dependence. This knowledge is crucial for properly interpreting and predicting magnetic properties in a wide range of materials, including those with heavy metal and magnetic layer interfaces. Additionally, the findings suggest that heavy metal layers can function as a means of inducing and controlling spin-orbit interaction in a controlled and proximal manner. This discovery opens up possibilities for exploring and manipulating magnetic anisotropy and its temperature dependence, which could lead to the design of innovative magnetic materials and devices, especially those utilizing the spin-orbit interaction, such as magnetic tunnel junctions, magnetic random access memory, and spin-orbit torque oscillators. This research also demonstrates the value of experimental and theoretical collaboration, which is essential for a comprehensive understanding of the complex interactions involved and for developing suitable models to describe these interactions. We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimization problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularization. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. The selected norms' impact on the model's performance is notable, as swapping certain norms was shown to switch the model's performance from excellent to very poor. The underlying mechanics of how enforcing a limited Lipschitz constant affects the model's performance, specifically its impact on the output's intermediate representations, was also investigated and these findings are presented in the paper. The code used in our experiments is publicly available on GitHub. The paper discusses the limitations of our approach, presents possible directions for further improvement, and offers a specific example of how enforcing a limited Lipschitz constant affects the model's performance on a particular dataset. The paper concludes by outlining three main contributions: (1) the development of a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, (2) the benefits of regularizing neural networks by enforcing a limited Lipschitz constant, and (3) the results of examining the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The paper is organized as follows: the introduction provides an overview of the importance of investigating input sensitivity in neural networks, the background on input sensitivity and Lipschitz continuity, and the motivation for developing a way to regularize neural networks by enforcing a limited Lipschitz constant. The next section explains the approach used to train neural networks with a limited Lipschitz constant, the section after that presents the results of experiments conducted to investigate the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance, and the final section concludes the paper. We investigate the production of same-sign lepton pairs via vector leptoquarks in third-generation models, focusing on theoretical predictions that incorporate the effects of quantum chromodynamics and electroweak interactions up to the next-to-leading order with particle-level simulations. Our analysis prioritizes the QCD contributions to Drell-Yan processes, which are central to detecting vector leptoquarks through scattering data. By comparing our results to available predictions, we reveal the importance of incorporating the impact of soft gluon fluctuations, which can be as substantial as 60% in certain scenarios. Furthermore, we establish scalable equations to calculate the rapidity distributions of the lepton pairs, accounting for the influence of mass terms and rare same-sign combinations. As vector leptoquarks couple to left- or right-handed fermions, we distinguish between long-lived particles that can be identified via large lepton rapidities or same- or opposite-helicity combinations, respectively. In cases where massless or light top-quark contributions are relevant, we analyze the impact of these effects on the scattering patterns. As such interactions deviate from standard model behaviors, we outline methods for extracting vector leptoquark information from scattering data, along with estimates for necessary luminosities at various particle colliders. The center of a discourse entity refers to the point where it is most integral to the overall scene, and a given sentence's connection to that scene is determined by this center. Our research investigates the connection between coreference resolution and the way entities are linked to the scene, using a neural network approach. We establish a dataset-specific metric that considers the relationship between a sentence and the scene's center, and demonstrate how effectively it captures the coreference resolution performance. Furthermore, we show that incorporating features related to the scene's center into our neural network-based coreference resolution system leads to an improvement in accuracy. Our findings also highlight the diversity of the dataset and the challenges it presents. We propose a simple method to handle polymorphic references and demonstrate its benefits. Our research provides a foundation for exploring the complex connections between the scene's center and coreference resolution. We make our code and datasets available at https://github.com/ghruvoi/centered.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains their maximum power that can be achieved for driving radio-frequency systems. In energy recovery linacs, where a beam travels in both directions, this problem is particularly complex due to beam interaction at the RF cavities. Studies have shown that the filling design significantly affects the beam breakup instability and that properly designed fill patterns could mitigate the problem. However, the impact of design variations has not been thoroughly explored. In this research, we investigated how different cavity placement designs within a period influence beam breakup instability. Our findings indicate that designs variation can result in up to 200 percent improvement in average power limit. Furthermore, we observed a 20 percent power limit gain from adopting a non-uniform period length. By integrating multiple period designs, researchers can achieve an average power limit gain of 400 percent. Moreover, our results demonstrated that the average power limit gains can be achieved without compromising for particle loss due to beam breakup instability. Lastly, we found that properly chosen designs could reduce the required aperture size, further enhancing the stability. In conclusion, carefully selecting a filling design is crucial for achieving the desired power in energy recovery linacs, and our study provides a framework for exploring and identifying optimal designs. Although our analysis was applied to an energy recovery linac, the associated theory is applicable to other accelerators that incorporate counter-rotating beams. In addition, we explored alternatives filling patterns such as re-arranging the beam trajectory at the RF cavity or using non-circular cavities. These possibilities open up new avenues for exploring ways to overcome beam breakup instability. Lastly, our research highlighted the significance of collaboration between particle accelerator experts and mathematicians in resolving various challenges faced by the community. In particular, we believe our work can be beneficial in addressing issues related to beam breakup instability in storage rings used for high-energy particle collisions. In addition, our findings can be applied to other problems that involve nonlinear analysis and counter-rotating beams. In this research, we examine the six-gluon scattering amplitude in $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory through the lens of color-ordered amplitude components. Focusing on the two-central-emission configurations, we derive the one-loop CEV for each case. Additionally, we contrast our findings with relevant two-gluon combinations of the six-gluon tree-level amplitude, demonstrating that the two-central-emission configurations can be interconnected by two gluons. Our work builds upon a prior discovery displaying the six-gluon scattering amplitude's intricate structure. Moreover, we present a customized integral reduction method that employs the six-gluon scattering amplitude's symmetric properties to simplify its one-loop CEV determination. Existing approaches, such as the six-gluon scattering amplitude's $\mathcal{N}=\infty$ supersymmetry, are utilized to validate our results. Furthermore, we explore implications of our research for six-gluon scattering amplitude properties, such as its two-gluon-mermaid diagram component. Existing data on six-gluon scattering amplitude components are updated, and new relations between six-gluon scattering amplitude components in $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory and $\mathcal{N}=4$ Yang-Mills four-point amplitude are derived. These relations demonstrate equivalence between two-gluon-mermaid diagrams in $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory and $\mathcal{N}=4$ Yang-Mills four-point amplitude. Similarly, another relation is presented which connects two-gluon-cusp diagrams in $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory and $\mathcal{N}=4$ Yang-Mills four-point amplitude. Another important finding of our research is the six-gluon scattering amplitude's two-gluon-mermaid diagram component nontrivially contributes to six-gluon scattering amplitude's two-gluon-cusp diagram component through two gluons. This contribution is demonstrated by equating two-gluon-cusp and two-gluon-mermaid diagram components in two separate relations, one for general case and another for the case where two gluons form a cusp. In the latter case, another relation is presented which connects two-gluon-cusp and two-gluon-mermaid diagram components directly. Another significant result of our research is the six-gluon scattering amplitude's two-gluon-mermaid diagram component's one-loop CEV

The metric dimension of a graph measures the minimum number of markers required to accurately pinpoint any vertex within the graph. In the context of evolving graphs, the problem becomes more complex, as we need to determine the minimum number of markers that must be positioned at various vertices across the graph's evolution, in order to pinpoint any vertex that may appear in the future graph. Here, we focus on a related problem known as the trimmed metric dimension, where the future graphs that can be pinpointed using a given set of markers are restricted to those derived from a specific subgraph of the original graph. Our key contributions in this paper include developing algorithms for determining the trimmed metric dimension of both static and evolving graphs, as well as examining the relationship between this dimension and other similar parameters such as the trimmed resolving number. Additionally, we provide specific formulas for certain types of static graphs, and demonstrate that one particular approach to calculating the trimmed metric dimension may be applied to dynamic graphs, although it requires examination of all possible combinations of vertices in the original graph. Our findings related to static graphs show that the trimmed resolving number of a tree is equal to its diameter, whereas in the context of dynamic graphs, we establish an upper bound for the trimmed metric dimension of an evolving tree. In both cases, we provide illustrative examples to demonstrate the applicability of these results. In contrast to other similar parameters, which often exhibit a polynomial relationship with the size of the graph, we show that the trimmed resolving number of a random graph typically exhibits an exponential relationship with the size of the graph, based on either Erdős-Rényi or Erdős-Rényi scale-free models. Our key contribution here is the application of a branching process, which provides a clear overview of the parameters governing the scaling properties of the trimmed resolving number. Our findings are supported by a combination of empirical studies and mathematical analysis. Researchers have successfully applied machine learning on all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope for its large data set, specifically the 10-year Pass8 event list. By utilizing K-means clustering and t-Distributed Density-based Spatial Clustering of Applications with High Dimensions, they have created detailed visualizations of the telescope's sensitivity and data collection patterns. A significant finding highlights variations in data collection patterns, likely caused by solar activity, Earth's magnetism, and atmospheric interference, which could be important considerations for future experiments. Additionally, machine learning has facilitated the identification of sources with irregular brightness, such as blazars, and has pinpointed approximately 1,000 unknown variable sources, primarily located in the galactic plane, which demonstrate patterns of radiation emission that could be linked to known populations of accreting compact objects, molecular clouds, and young star-forming regions. Further analysis of these sources, combined with multi-wavelength data, is necessary to confirm these findings. All results have been made available through interactive visualizations on Fermi Facts.

While this type of configuration is uncommon, it is expected to occur about 1.4% of the time for a random pair of asteroids.  Throughout the survey, we found 147 pairs of asteroids that could be distinguished from background and field contamination, with 13 pairs exhibiting a luminosity ratio greater than 10 to 1.  However, only 3 pairs exhibited a luminosity ratio within 1.5 to 1, which is indicative of true binary asteroids.  We analyzed these 3 pairs, all of which were located in the outer solar system, particularly in the orbits of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. In this paper, we explore a partially linear regression model, which combines a parametric component and a non-parametric component. We then demonstrate how to estimate the parameters of this model, including the coefficients of the covariates and the non-parametric component, specifically the average treatment effect. We also establish theoretical properties for consistent estimation, including the covariates' coefficients and the average treatment effect. Furthermore, we provide proofs of asymptotic normality for these estimators. Additionally, we examine how peer influences within a network can be estimated and provide an empirical example utilizing a random forest peer influence model. Lastly, we offer an appendix containing additional mathematical proofs.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It applies a modified version of the Leibniz Rule to solve a class of fractional differential equations. A key example is provided to illustrate using the new Leibniz Rule in solving a specific type of fractional differential equation. Furthermore, comparisons are drawn with existing formulae, demonstrating the novelty of our approach. Additionally, a discussion on the application to the fractional variational calculus is given. A novel approach to the Bateman fractional derivative is also presented. This study's results can be utilized in a wide range of applications, including in geophysics, economics, and biology. A particular feature of this approach is its ability to handle negative and fractional orders, which has been previously unaddressed in the literature.
