We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how language guidance can be used to advance theory-of-mind and intentions understanding, which are critical components of human communication. We create a massive Dungeons and Dragons dataset with nearly 20,000 conversations, incorporating over 10,000 theoretical scenarios that require players to navigate complex social situations, characteristic of D&D world-building. Our approach to guiding conversations through intended actions yields promising results, surpassing non-guided discussions in problem-solving, adventure-world creation, and character development. In particular, we find that players who receive guidance develop their intentions at a faster rate, while those who don't tend to get lost in the process. Interestingly, we observe that players who excel at D&D without a Dungeon Master also perform poorly under guided conversations, suggesting a dispositive metric for identifying experienced players. Our work concludes with an analysis of why guided conversations are essential tools for instructors, offering actionable insights to enhance teaching, learning, and communication. The G4C dataset, available for public use, presents numerous opportunities for advancement in areas like intent and theory-of-mind detection, counterfactual generation, and action-oriented dialogue.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the bending modes of knotted proteins based on a topological representation, offering a precise graphical outline of their structure. By utilizing magnetic resonance imaging, researchers have successfully mapped the 3D architecture of various knotted proteins, including their slow dynamics and rigid elements. A novel approach using persistence diagrams and a voting system was developed to determine the most prevalent bending modes within native states of proteins, even those that are twisted into complex knots such as trefoil and Christian knots. A comparative analysis of different proteins reveals a predominant straightening pathway - a pattern that holds true across all proteins studied and suggests a universally adopted protein folding strategy. Furthermore, a unique approach was discovered for the protein Ribonuclease A, which is knotted in a unique way called the Christian knot, offering a distinctive perspective on its folding and binding dynamics. The developed framework also enables the detection of anomalous bending modes, as seen in the slowly folding protein carbonic anhydrase II. The introduced concept of a topological selection of bending modes can be expanded to other complex systems, offering a genuine view of their intrinsic topology that is unaffected by various measurement approaches. A novel mechanism for converting spinless atoms into molecules is proposed, leveraging laser-induced three-body recombination.  This process, which occurs when two spinless atoms collide after being excited by a laser, can result in the creation of a single molecule along with two spin-1/2 particles rather than three.  Our calculations indicate that this process is feasible with currently available technology, and that it favors the production of molecules in specific channels.  Furthermore, it is anticipated that this process could be steered toward converting spinless atoms into molecules of a particular symmetry through the use of focused laser beams, following a pattern that is determined by the angle of the beam.  This process, which is efficient and possesses a clear parameter dependence, is distinct from other atom-molecule conversion methods and may offer a novel means of coherent control over this process.  We have conducted comprehensive simulations of this process, providing a detailed understanding of its components and demonstrating that it is capable of converting a substantial portion of the initial atom population into molecules.  We have also explored various experimental configurations, presenting numerical data on the molecules' spin-dependent distribution, angular momentum, and symmetry.  These findings suggest that this process is not only capable of converting spinless atoms into molecules but also offers a means of controlling their quantum properties, and as such it has the potential to contribute to a broader goal of developing a quantum simulator that employs atom-molecule condensates.  We have previously reported this proposed research, presenting preliminary data on the process in a form of an abstract at an international conference.  This paper represents a more comprehensive report on this research, incorporating new numerical data that we have obtained since then. Our proposed DNA-storage system addresses two major challenges in previous DNA-data structures.  First, no existing solution provides a efficient way to create a hierarchical organization from user data, as current methods have a significant overhead in encoding recursive relationships.  Second, no system can efficiently handle data updates in previous DNA-storage approaches.  Our solution introduces a novel, self-replicating marker that enables efficient encoding of hierarchical relationships and simplifies the process of creating a hierarchical structure.  Additionally, we demonstrate that certain types of data updates can be performed quickly and easily, without the need to re-write the entire storage.  Our evaluation shows that our approach offers a significant improvement over existing methods, offering a 10 times speed increase in encoding recursive relationships and a 3 times speed increase in data updates.  We also show that our system provides a high level of flexibility in handling various data updates.  Our findings are further validated through a real-world implementation of a hierarchical DNA storage.  Our system, named DNA-Hier, is available online.

This study conducts a comprehensive comparison of state-of-the-art algebraic solvers for solving the discretized equations originating from cardiac mechanics models, specifically focusing on the total finite element stiffness and mass matrices, and the algebraic representation of blood pressure in a cardiac chamber. We examined and computed with 3D cardiac mechanics models involving left ventricle blood chambers, utilizing different solver combinations such as direct methods, multigrid techniques, balancing domain decomposition, and GMRES iterative solvers, both with and without preconditioning. Our study reveals that the most effective solvers vary depending on whether the goal is to accurately depict blood pressure or efficiently solve the discretized equations. We found that the most precise pressure predictions resulted from a combination of PARDISO and MUMPS solvers, whereas the most computationally efficient approach for modeling the mechanics of the cardiac chamber was a combination of PARDISO and BDDC/GLS solvers. Our results also demonstrate the distinct impacts of different solvers on blood pressure estimates and highlight the significance of thoroughly testing and validating numerical models through pressure sensitivity analysis. Our study includes an introductory overview, along with mathematical foundations of the problem, but focuses primarily on the results of our computations. We conclude with a discussion of our findings, presenting the most promising solver combinations for large-scale cardiac mechanics simulations, together with important practical implications for researchers and scientists working in the field. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. This study examines a one-dimensional cyclic transport equation featuring periodic advection, where particles move in a closed system. Cyclic transport occurs when the system is designed to return to its original state after a set period of time. We investigate the long-term behavior of a nonlinear transport model with periodic boundary conditions. By applying a compactness argument, we demonstrate the existence of solutions that converge to a steady state. Additionally, we identify conditions under which these solutions are cyclic. However, we also find that these solutions can experience singularities, despite being periodic. This discovery is significant because it refutes a previous conjecture stating that solutions to the cyclic transport equation are necessarily smooth. Furthermore, we provide examples of both smooth and singular solutions to the equation. In these cases, we also investigate the long-term behavior of the solutions, demonstrating that they converge to a specific steady state called a delta-function supported on a moving interval. This research also explores a related equation where the transport velocity is fixed and the transport equation becomes a nonlinear diffusion equation. We demonstrate that solutions to this equation can experience singularities, which in turn cause the formation of a delta-function supported on a moving interval. This causes the transport velocity to shift and become cyclic. This discovery is significant because it provides insight into the formation of delta-functions and their role in shifting and becoming cyclic. This finding also demonstrates that even when the transport equation is constrained to a fixed interval, it can still experience singularities, which in turn causes the transport to become cyclic. This behavior is unique and has not been previously observed. In the final section of this paper, we examine a related question involving the transport equation and present a lower bound for the time it takes for the solution to experience a singularity. This bound is based on a previous result developed by Bembom, Herrington, and Kiselev, as well as a compactness argument. This research expands on previous work by providing a new scenario in which the solution experiences a singularity and offering a more detailed analysis of this scenario. This paper also includes three appendices that contain additional information relevant to the results of this research. Appendix A discusses the development of the model used in this study, while Appendix B examines the behavior of the solutions to the transport equation, including the formation of a delta-function, and Appendix C provides a comparison between the solutions to the transport equation and the solutions to the nonlinear diffusion equation. This research expands on previous work by providing a new scenario in which the solution experiences a singularity and offering a more detailed analysis of this scenario.

Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram. We demonstrate that specific non-equilibrium situations, marked by the onset of synchronization or sudden death, result in distinct patterns emerging in the optical tomogram. These distinctive patterns cannot be replicated by arbitrary state preparations, effectively serving as signatures that can be physically assessed, even in an ideal scenario. Our study focuses on two non-equilibrium situations: the collapse of entanglement between two coupled systems and a pair undergoing synchronization. We show that in these cases, the relationship between the points of variation in the optical tomogram and the parameters that characterize the change can be deduced through analytical calculations, thereby enabling the reliable prediction of the associated patterns. Conversely, in more complicated scenarios, where the dynamics are influenced by decoherence and the state is no longer Gaussian, we employ a machine learning approach, specifically multilayer perceptrons, to anticipate the associated patterns. 360-degree virtual tourism videos provide an immersive view of destinations but present a significant challenge in predicting the optimal viewing angle due to their extensive field of view. By focusing on videos from popular tourism spots, research has shown that people tend to follow specific patterns in their viewpoint, which can be informed by their previous knowledge and personal interests. Despite the potential benefits of automatic perspective prediction, only a few approaches have been proposed, and existing methods often rely on expensive and hard-to-acquire annotation data. This paper introduces a novel technique for perspective prediction that trains a single hidden layer neural network using only publicly available video subtitle information, which serves as a surrogate for the viewer's prior knowledge and interests. Experimental results show that this method outperforms the baseline in various evaluation metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of using subtitle-based knowledge for prediction. As the problem domain lacks standard evaluation protocols, further exploration of different evaluation methods is required to fully assess the model's performance. The proposed approach provides a promising foundation for future research in subtitle-based feature extraction and more comprehensive evaluation strategies. The code is available online at https://github.com/ChengmingInnovation/Prediction-for-360-degree-Video.

Our primary goal is to demonstrate the existence of a uniformly decoupling family of curves that are embedded within these surfaces and satisfy certain non-planarity conditions. Our proof relies on a combination of the Eisenstein's theorem, the Fefferman's tube theorem, and the development of a set of approximation surfaces that effectively partition the original surface. Furthermore, we offer a numerical example that illustrates our findings. Additionally, our research yields a related inequality related to the surface's Euler characteristic. Lastly, our results can be viewed as a refinement of a prior finding by the same authors. Utilizing a non-singular expansion, we evaluated the correlation function for two color dipole operators, finding that it is analogous to the exponential of a Bessel function, which is relevant for investigating higher-order azimuthal distributions. Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. For modules with a simple and intuitive lattice structure, such as regular representations of certain groups, this task can be automated. However, even for relatively small representation groups, their lattice structures often prove difficult to determine automatically. In the case of the Coxeter group Sn, which consists of permutations represented as cycles, we have an alternative approach that involves analyzing the cycle structures of its elements. Specifically, we define a set of rules that can be applied to the cycle structures, allowing us to determine the lattice structure of its module lattice. We have successfully implemented this approach to calculate the lattice structure for the module lattice associated with the group S6. Notably, our approach yields unique results for a specific subgroup of Wreth-Thompson group, which cannot be determined using other methods. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a novel Co-Imitation Training (CIT) framework that generates informative supervisory signals from suboptimal agents performing the task, thereby obtaining the benefits of imitation learning at a fraction of the cost. The CIT approach achieves this by leveraging the contrasting experiences of successful and failing agents to create a risk-aware value function, which is then utilized to direct them towards a successful outcome. We have thoroughly evaluated the CIT framework across a range of challenging tasks and scenarios, including complex robotic manipulation, multi-agent competition, and difficult single-agent challenges. The resulting data demonstrates notable enhancements in performance when compared to both non-imitation and non-co-imitation methods, showcasing the CIT framework's versatility and effectiveness. The code for this research is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ChengxiangCao/Co-Imitation-Training.

In large-scale neural machine translation, the action space can be very extensive, making the exploration-exploitation trade-off even more challenging. We analyze the connection between action space size and the neural network's output, showing that the large action space leads to overfitting, continuous output values, and difficulty in convergence. To address this issue, we propose a novel exploration method, a new training objective, and a strategy to increase the embedding dimension. We also explore the impact of clipping the output values, showing that a carefully designed architecture can manage large action spaces with minimal adjustment. In our experiments, using a transformer encoder-decoder to model the data, we find that our exploration method, training objective, and proposed architecture enhancements consistently improve the sequence-level BLEU scores across three translation datasets. We also compare our methods to existing exploration techniques, finding that our approaches outperform the alternatives by significant margins. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for various isolation levels in its concurrency control mechanism. Despite its prevalence, there is limited information available about the theoretical foundations of MongoDB's transactional coherence. In fact, a previous study classified its coherence property as unknown. This paper fills this knowledge gap by conducting an in-depth analysis of MongoDB's transactional coherence. Specifically, we determine that MongoDB's coherence property corresponds to a particular feature of PVZIs (Possibly Valid Zero-Insertion States), which is called weak visibility. This property can be achieved through a validation process known as type soundness. Furthermore, we find that MongoDB's isolation levels correspond to specific variants of weak visibility known as visibility. Moreover, we establish that MongoDB's type soundness is directly linked to its visibility, and that this relationship holds true across its various implementations. Lastly, we provide a concrete example of a MongoDB store configuration. The approach we took in this research involves formally defining MongoDB's semantics using a type and validation system, which provides a clear and verifiable understanding of the database's transactional coherence. This representation can be utilized as a baseline for any future extensions or variations of MongoDB. Our analysis shows that the assembly's stability can be predicted by calculating a topological invariant known as the Euler characteristic of the network's configuration, which is conserved over time as the system changes due to thermal fluctuations. By taking into account the assembly's concealed geometry, our research reveals that the Euler characteristic's conservation law must be modified to include a random rotation component associated with the fluctuations. Researchers studying the dynamics of an isolated, expanding universe have discovered that it contains an intense, shrinking spherical shell of matter. This shell is coterminus with a hollow, expanding sphere of space. The fast-moving outer layer of the shell undergoes sonic acceleration, resulting in a highly nonlinear, oscillatory and ultimately asymptotic state of affairs. Contrary to expectations, even when accounting for the effects of an isolated universe, self-similar solutions to the Euler equations in an expanding universe do not necessarily require the curvature of geodesics to be small. In fact, when there is little curvature, the solutions exhibit an exponentially decreasing asymptotic behavior, as opposed to the commonly held view that they should have a power-law decline. Additionally, it has been found that even in an open, isolated universe, there is no such thing as a stable, expanding shock; instead, it breaks into an oscillatory state. All possible scenarios are represented in figures to aid in visualization. The study relies on a custom-made, conservative self-similar scheme that maintains the conservative properties of the Euler equations and accurately determines the asymptotic behavior of the solutions. A new class of potential operators with hermitian properties is defined using generalized Hermite polynomials. These polynomials are identified and analyzed, and their key properties, including generating functions and expansion formulas, are determined. Consequentially, a set of quasi-exactly solvable Schrödinger equations is obtained, and their corresponding bound state energies and related wave functions are extracted. Notably, these results demonstrate a previously unknown connection between generalized Hermite polynomials and solvable quantum mechanics. Moreover, a transformation rule for these polynomials is obtained, leading to a derivation of the classical Gaussian distribution. Finally, these results are applied to a family of potentials characterized by their hyperspherical coordinate equivalents, and the underlying monodromy-free Schrödinger operator spectrum is explicitly defined. This potential operator class includes a linear potential, a position-dependent mass Pöschl-Teller potential, and a Coulomb potential in three-dimensional space, among others. These results also yield exact solutions for a related Hamiltonian operator defined on a semi-line segment. This research was originally published in Eur. Phys. J. C. Vol. 83, 2023.

Surprisingly, finding the shortest distance between two points in a self-organizing map representation of the sound waves revealed a uniform value, which remained constant regardless of peeling speed or pressure. This constant value can be used as a metric to compare the randomness of other time-series data. In the course of the experiment, varying the adhesive tape's surface tension led to changes in noise patterns, which were reflected in the maps, yet the pattern of points remained consistent with a particular mathematical relationship. It is hypothesized that it could be an expression of the underlying structure of human perception, which has been debated among scientists for centuries. The question of whether the data reflects a genuine physical property or a feature of the analysis method remains to be determined, as it was demonstrated that the same pattern can be found in other random processes generated by different methods, including chaotic systems, fractals, and self-organized crowds. A key finding in this model reveals that, when current opportunities are unevenly distributed, earlier generations have more influence over the outcomes of later generations. Additionally, as time passes, the impact of a fair initial distribution of children's ability dimensions diminishes, while the effect of a fair initial distribution of educational opportunities does the opposite. It is also discovered that greater mobility is associated with a more significant impact of children's ability dimensions and a lesser impact of educational opportunities on the outcomes of later generations. We introduce a novel cluster structure on the basis of quantum groups, which is linked to Lusztig's original algebraic structure. This new structure is utilized to derive properties of quantum cluster algebras, particularly the character of the quantum group U_q(\g) for Lie algebras of type A-D. This leads to a demonstration that the quantum group U_q(\g) contains a subalgebra isomorphic to the Laurent polynomial extension of the parent algebra, with the latter being constructed from the cluster structure. A related presentation of the quantum group U_q(\g) is also obtained, along with an associated cluster automorphism. Lastly, we show that the structure of quantum groups allows for the construction of related cluster algebras, which include the quantum tori, providing an alternative perspective on the latter. Recently launched on the Ethereum network, Forsage has been touted as the world's first "decentralized network without requirements," allowing users to participate freely. However, our in-depth investigation into the network's operations reveals a complex web of deceptive tactics designed to mislead users and swindle them out of their cryptocurrency. At its core, Forsage represents a type of pyramid scheme, in which new investors are constantly needed to keep the system afloat, with users located globally, despite the lack of anonymity. We uncover the intricate mechanisms underlying this scheme, including customized smart contracts that ensure the scammer walks away with the majority of the funds, as the network's operators exploit a loophole in Ethereum's functionality known as "reentrancy." Furthermore, we identify key individuals associated with Forsage, revealing that it is not a decentralized network, but rather controlled by a small group of people with significant influence. The total amount of money lost to Forsage is substantial, with estimates suggesting it exceeds $300 million. The case of Forsage offers a sobering reminder of the risks involved in participating in cryptocurrency projects, as well as the critical importance of conducting thorough due diligence before engaging with them. The network's operations also raise significant security concerns, as we demonstrate how it is possible to reverse the flow of Ethereum funds, which could have far-reaching implications for developing secure smart contract designs. The extensive research we conducted into Forsage may also be useful in creating anti-scam strategies, as well as providing a detailed analysis of the network's architecture, smart contracts, and the Ethereum loop-hole that it exploits. The findings presented in this paper have been visually represented in a supplementary appendix available online. The growth and operations of Forsage may seem complex and difficult to comprehend, but we believe that understanding its mechanics and the challenges it poses is crucial, which is why we have made the research available to the public in the hope that it may aid in preventing similar scams from occurring in the future. The case of Forsage also raises important questions about the role of social media platforms, the challenges of identifying and reporting scams, and the risks involved in participating in cryptocurrency projects, as well as the significance of developing secure smart contract designs, which are all explored in a companion blog available online. The research conducted into Forsage may also be of interest to scholars in the fields of sociology and anthropology, as well as to cryptocurrency enthusiasts, as well as anyone interested in the human factors involved in scams. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. For each candidate, we calculated key astrophysical properties including mass, radius, luminosity, surface temperature, metallicity, and age. However, only three clusters met the requirements to have their metallicities determined but not their ages, leading us to re-examine the metallicity determination process. We found that [Fe/H] correlations were based on limited data and we derived new estimates averaging results from several studies. Additionally, we calculated metallicity distributions using two methods including a simple average and considering study weights, both yielding similar outcomes. Furthermore, we encountered three clusters with similar characteristics to the galaxy's halo clusters, possessing higher luminosities than expected and potentially being distant globular clusters similar to those found in the galaxy's halo rather than those located in the galaxy's bulge. We have presented detailed findings for each cluster and contributed new data on the galaxy's bulge cluster population. Furthermore, we have incorporated the results into the catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters, now consisting of over a hundred confirmed members. The catalog, in addition to standard properties, also includes spatial distribution information and varies in terms of metallicity distributions. Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process, determined by event quantities and case
completion times, thereby providing valuable insights into their behavior under
different process conditions. Our experiments surprisingly reveal that the basic
Multi-layer Perceptron frequently surpasses more advanced deep learning models
in both prediction tasks. Consequently, when deploying predictive process models,
due caution is required as they perform differently across various process stages
and it's also advisable to establish results with strong baselines like simple
Multi-layer Perceptron. Our code is available at https://github.com/DeepProcessMining/Business-Process-Prediction.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. The predictions are based on semi-empirical models of temperature and optical depth and are validated through comparisons with observed spectra. The results show that the simulations accurately replicate the balance between electron-scattering and hydrogen line broadening in the line-free continuum of $\lambda \approx 2200-2800$ Å\  but find that the flux of this line-free continuum is significantly greater than previously estimated, which has important implications for assessing bio-signatures in exoplanetary atmospheres affected by low mass star environments in the near-ultraviolet. Furthermore, the simulations provide a previously unreported Balmer jump shift in the continuum of $\lambda \approx 2800-3000$ Å\  that can be used as a diagnostic for the balance between electron-scattering and hydrogen line broadening. The code used for these simulations is being made publicly available to facilitate assessments of exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low mass stars' UV environments. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/krishna-singh88/adleo_flares. The data associated with this study are available at https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/search/q?project=hea&order=filter&filter=author:%22Krishna%20Singh%22. The findings of this research have been published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, Volume 495, Issue 1, 2020, pp. e14, ISSN 0035-871X, doi: 10.1093/mnras/staa745. The current code version used for the simulations is v1.0. The code is written in Python 3.7. The code depends on the following packages: numpy 1.19.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulative attacks that misguide them. To fortify these models against deceptive inputs, researchers propose a novel technique called Transformation-Point Cloud Smoothing (TPS), a differentiable method that smooths out distorted point clouds by preserving key topological characteristics. Unlike other denoising techniques that rely on geometric metrics, TPS leverages transformation invariance, a property unique to neural network-based latent representations. Utilizing TPS as a module in a larger network, researchers demonstrated an increase in robustness in both real-world 3D object classification and synthetic navigation scenarios, without sacrificing accuracy. Furthermore, in some cases, this technique outperformed more complex and computationally expensive alternatives. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/ghr95/TPC.

In this research, we develop an innovative clustering approach called Impact Based Clustering (IBC) to analyze complex systems whose behavior varies over time. Unlike traditional methods that focus on modeling dynamics, IBC extracts insights from time-series data by identifying distinct patterns of influence. We utilize two key sources of information: correlation matrices derived from time-series data and graph theory. Specifically, we utilize the connectivity of a network to determine the clustering structure, while the graph's layout provides valuable information on data patterns. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of IBC, which has been successfully applied to a financial index and a global climate model. Furthermore, IBC demonstrates a way to deal with the dimensionality reduction challenge, which is a common issue in data analysis. We make available our IBC code on GitHub. Additionally, we provide a climate-based forecasting model as an extension to the IBC approach. This model, called Data-Driven Autoregressive Multiresolution Clustering (DDARMuC), offers a novel method for predicting complex systems by leveraging their internal structure and resistance to noise. DDARMuC has been successfully applied to a critical test case: forecasting global temperature patterns. This approach demonstrates a way to deal with the challenge of predicting complex systems through time-series analysis. We make available the DDARMuC code on GitHub. In recent years, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have gained significant traction in generating coherent and realistic text. Current GAN-based text generation algorithms focus primarily on training networks to create text that is both coherent and convincing. However, there is a lack of available research on GAN-based methods specifically designed to counter these coherent text generation models by producing misleading information. To address this imbalance, we present SparseGAN, a novel framework that simultaneously trains two antagonistic networks: a generative network to create convincing text and a discriminative network to identify fabricated information. The proposed model incorporates two key features that contribute to improved performance. Firstly, a new GAN-based loss function called the Reverse Loss Function (RLF) is introduced, which enables the generative network to differentiate between high-quality generated text and fabricated information. Secondly, the model incorporates a memory-based mechanism that allows the discriminative network to distinguish between various text categories. Experimental results on publicly available datasets demonstrate that the SparseGAN model excels in multiple assessment metrics over various baseline models. Furthermore, the proposed model demonstrates significant versatility, showcasing superior performance in other tasks such as text classification. The code for SparseGAN is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/ShubhamSinghDev/SparseGAN. The model has also been deployed as a web application at the following address: http://spargan.textgen.com/. The proposed RLF loss function has the potential to benefit various text generation tasks that involve evaluating the authenticity of text. The model's memory-based mechanism to distinguish between text categories could be adapted for other classification tasks. The proposed SparseGAN model offers numerous opportunities for further development, such as fine-tuning the memory-based mechanism, integrating the model with other text generation algorithms, and developing a more sophisticated evaluation metric that could be beneficial to the broader text generation community. The theory of interstellar panspermia suggests that microorganisms could be transported from one planetary system to another on comets, asteroids, or spacecraft. While this idea is intellectually engaging, it's challenging to verify this concept scientifically. Nevertheless, we can anticipate certain consequences if interstellar panspermia is genuine. For instance, it's likely that comet surfaces would exhibit signs of biological activity, and microorganisms would be present in certain types of meteorites. Furthermore, there's a possibility that extraterrestrial viruses could be capable of replicating on Earth, potentially even causing rare illnesses in astronauts. These indicators include specific comet surface features, types of meteorites harboring microorganisms, particular astronomical events that could disseminate microorganisms across space, and the composition of comet and meteorite samples. Animal population studies often aim to understand how animals interact with each other and their environment, including how they select resources and move within their habitat. While capture-recapture methods are effective for estimating population parameters and detecting animals, they do not account for resource choice or genetic exchange, whereas choice experiments and genetic data can provide this information but do not capture the full extent of animal interactions. Our research integrates capture-recapture analysis with choice experiments and genetic data to investigate how animals choose resources and interact with each other within their habitat. By combining models of resource choice, demography, and spatial genetics, we developed an method that can account for random movements as well as deliberate choice of resources, enabling us to estimate key population parameters including immigration rates, genetic exchange distances, and resource choice probabilities. Our approach allows researchers to recover important population metrics from capture-recapture data while also incorporating valuable information from choice experiments and genetic data. We applied and tested our method using simulated and real data, including genetic, choice, and capture-recapture data from a study of the greater sage-grouse. Our analysis revealed the importance of considering random movements, spatial autocorrelation, and resource choice in inferring population metrics, and was also able to provide a more detailed understanding of this species' habitat needs. Our study's findings have significant implications for managing and conserving populations and their habitats, and our method's versatility makes it suitable for a wide range of applications across various taxa. We have also explored management scenarios for the greater sage-grouse using our method and found that reducing habitat fragmentation and managing shrub cover according to the birds' preferred ranges could significantly increase their population sizes and reduce their risk of extinction. Our research highlights the importance of considering the complex interactions between animals and their environment, including resource choice and genetic exchange, in order to conserve populations and their habitats effectively. The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a better understanding by incorporating the interplay between different components, than a simple, single-network approach. However, the majority of current research focuses primarily on the dynamics of node interactions within each layer, without giving sufficient attention to the spreading process of specific phenomena across the network. This study focuses on the transmission of solutions in multilayer networks composed of oscillators, where the state of each layer follows the phase reduction model. By applying a new transmission model, we were able to investigate the spread of a given state $\Theta_0$ across the network. Our results show that the degree of node connection, rather than the specific multilayer topology, plays a significant role in determining the speed of state transmission. Additionally, we found that the state transmission can be predicted by a linear diffusion equation, where the effective diffusion layer $\Gamma$ is directly related to the degree distribution. Furthermore, we explored the impact of multilayer topology on state transmission, where the transition from a small-world multilayer network to a random multilayer network leads to a significant slowdown in state transmission. Moreover, we established a critical layer degree $\lambda_c$ below which the network becomes susceptible to the transmission of the Kessler-Buckingham scenario, where the distribution of the phase becomes bimodal. Our findings also suggest that the approach we developed can be applied to investigate the spread of other phenomena, such as synchronization or chaos, across multilayer networks. Our research was theoretically and numerically verified, where the agreement between the prediction of the transmission model and the actual observation of state transmission was found to be very high, with the exception of cases where the degree distribution changes suddenly, where the time it takes for the state to spread also changes suddenly, but does not match the prediction of the transmission model. The most effective linear solvers for matrix inversion are iterative methods, which achieve fast computation by minimizing the precision of intermediate results. However, when dealing with the inverse of a matrix in a scalar operation, such as matrix multiplication, these methods can become less efficient due to their complex structure. In response, we propose a novel approach based on the Neumann series, leveraging the precision of intermediate results to further optimize the calculation. For example, in the calculation of $x^T A^{-1} x$, we use the Neumann series to directly obtain the sum of the inverse elements of $A$ instead of computing $A^{-1}$ separately. To accommodate different matrix sizes and precision levels, we provide a formula that enables us to compare the number of operations required. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between our technique and existing fast iterative matrix inversion methods, finding that it can be viewed as a variant of the Wynn $\epsilon$-algorithm. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we show the equivalence of one previous method and the Wynn $\epsilon$-algorithm, and provide a related technique called the modified Neumann series. Additionally, we investigate the application of our method to matrices with a small condition number, and explore the relevant theoretical background. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises from the unpredictable nature of terrain. This challenge is magnified for monopod hopping, as it involves unstable phases of motion. To overcome this, a simulation environment incorporating realistic terrain profiles is crucial. We have developed a computational framework that accurately models terrains with the ability to simulate deformation in response to contact forces during monopod hopping. Using this simulator, we conducted a range of simulations covering various terrain types, including soft, friable, and cohesive soils. The resulting data were analyzed to identify key factors that influence hindrance to hopping, citing the effects of force depth, surface roughness, and surface slope. Furthermore, we demonstrated the applicability of our simulator in evaluating control strategies and robotic designs through a simple control test and a design evaluation for a hopping robot. The simulator is available as an open-source tool on GitHub, enabling the robotic and biomechanics communities to utilize it for their respective research needs. The data collected during our research are also publicly accessible on the MendeFLORE repository. The underlying challenge of dealing with uncertain terrain is also a critical issue for other locomotion methods, suggesting that our simulator could be adapted for their use cases. The proposed simulator offers a realistic simulation environment that responds accurately to the dynamics of monopod hopping, providing a valuable resource for biologists, biomechanicians, and engineers working with legged systems. Quantum annealing (QA) has the potential to solve complex optimization problems by leveraging coherent fluctuations, yet its effectiveness is hindered by the presence of bumps in the average fidelity. Notwithstanding this challenge, our research demonstrates that these fidelity bumps can be harnessed to provide valuable information about the problem's solution. Specifically, we show that in exact cover problems, the interval between fidelity bumps is directly related to the minimum number of qubits required to solve the problem. Furthermore, we find that this relationship can be determined through classical simulation of the quantum dynamics. As such, our approach allows us to efficiently identify an optimal quantum annealing parameter, bypassing the need for time-consuming and costly experimental measurements. In addition to this finding, we investigate the distinct features of quench dynamics in various regime of the interqubit coupling and uncover how dynamical phase transitions are reflected in the average fidelity. The resulting analysis provides a set of universal thresholds that define different evolutionary phases of the quench dynamics. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through the quantum annealing of a real-world exact cover problem containing 5 logical qubits. The underlying principles are anticipated to have broader implications for the quantum optimization of various models. The code used for simulations is publicly available on GitHub. The experimental setup and associated data are also publicly available on the D-Wave Quantum Cloud. Our research examined the impact of charge carrier screening on the onset of a canted magnetic phase in a hypothetical infinite-layer nickelate using theoretical modeling. This study was a follow-up to previous work that found the magnetic phase ordering to be driven by proximity to an antiferromagnetic state due to screening of the Coulomb interaction. We discovered that this material might exhibit unconventional superconductivity, as predicted by theoretical models that suggest it has a d+id-wave symmetry. To further understand infinite-layer nickelate, we investigated its two-dimensional equivalents and found that the 120-degree canted magnetic phase could arise from competition between on-site and adjacent site Coulomb interactions. This could be confirmed by experiments that detect the magnetic structure, while local and adjacent site bond distributions of spin and charge could provide insight into the screening of Coulomb interactions. Furthermore, we analyzed the relationship between on-site and adjacent site Coulomb interactions and screening of the Coulomb interaction, and how these interactions influence the ground states of infinite-layer nickelate. Notably, one of these scenarios, which involves the presence of strange quarks in neutron star matter, has been found to be supported by recent observational data of neutron stars. In this context, investigating the sound speed in dense matter is crucial, as it can help in better understanding the density distribution of neutron stars. Our analysis indicates that the sound speed becomes super-luminous at high densities of neutron stars matter, which is a critical observation that can be influenced by the presence of hyperons, quark matter, or other factors. Furthermore, studies based on relativistic mean-field models that include baryons, mesons, and kaon mesons, but exclude strange quarks, cannot accurately describe the sound speed in high-density neutron stars matter. This finding has significant implications for the four-times reduced chi-squared per degree of freedom ($\chi^2/d.o.f.$) obtained from recent analyses of neutron stars. High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. However, the effect of a specific post-Newtonian parameter, $\gamma$, which affects angular distance measurements, has a significant impact when calculating positions and distances of stars with a high degree of precision. Our study examines the impact of the $\gamma$ parameter's uncertainty on measurements obtained from a mock Gaia-like telescope, with a focus on its influence on parallax measurements. We found that the uncertainty in $\gamma$ is a crucial factor in determining the precision of parallax measurements, especially for closer stars. For a value of $\gamma$ equal to 1.001, the change in the average parallax precision of stars within a megaparsec is almost negligible, around 0.06 milliseconds of arc. Furthermore, we found that the precision of angular distance measurements decreases significantly further from the megaparsec scale, where the effect of $\gamma$ uncertainty becomes negligible. Therefore, the precision of parallax measurements from a telescope like Gaia will primarily be limited by other factors rather than the $\gamma$ parameter's uncertainty. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven multi-stage approach, tailored for open-domain question answering. Within this approach, an initial coarse guess is made based on widely applicable knowledge, followed by a series of refinements guided by the underlying semantics. As the answer is iteratively refined, it draws upon more specialized knowledge that is increasingly relevant to the question at hand. To validate our approach, we present comprehensive experiments across a range of question-answering benchmarks, revealing consistent improvements over benchmarks that require general knowledge and notable gains over several baselines in open-domain question answering. Notably, our approach secures a superior score on the Scientific_Evidence_Reading_Comprehension benchmark, demonstrating the value of our approach in assessing the credibility of statements. Moreover, we provide a pre-trained model that is available for public use. Code and model availability: https://github.com/THU-CLG/Coarse-To-Careful.

A comprehensive review is presented of existing observations of cometary cations, with a focus on those featuring oxygen and highlighting the scientific value that could be derived from additional observations. A predicted composite spectrum of a comet showcasing the mentioned cations is also provided, along with a historical context of prominent oxygen-containing molecular cations observed in space, with particular emphasis on cations that have been studied both theoretically and experimentally. In the context of a client-server learning model, where clients with access to sensitive data and a remote server with limited data participate in a learning process, we explore a new framework for randomized feedforward learning. This framework leverages a combination of local and server-based algorithms, incorporating both stochastic gradient descent and random walk techniques. Specifically, clients engage in a learning process through randomized walk, triggered by significant deviations in performance, thereby reducing communication with the server. This process enables clients to explore their local models independently, adapting to new data without further communication with the server. Our theoretical analysis, complemented by experimental results on synthetic and real-world data, demonstrates that this approach yields superior performance compared to conventional randomized feedforward learning. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/learning-at-infinity/Random-Walk.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique called Consistency via Overlapping Areas (COA) to address such labeling limitations. The proposed approach ensures consistency across areas within the image that should be consistently labeled as similar, thereby utilizing the unannotated regions to constrain the model's output. The resulting algorithm is computationally efficient and easily integrable into existing optimization pipelines. Experimental evaluations using both simulated and real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness of COA, showing it outperforms alternative comparison methods across various metrics. In a world where complex quantum systems can behave unpredictably, even for small numbers of particles, a new approach using graph neural networks has successfully interpreted the underlying dynamics of these systems. By applying a technique called time-fed graph neural networks, researchers were able to analyze a crucial phenomenon called the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which demonstrates the unpredictable nature of quantum behavior. In a breakthrough, they uncovered the precise conditions under which this principle breaks down, revealing a graphical pattern that indicates the onset of chaos. To validate their findings, the researchers simulated a well-known model called the Jaynes-Cummings model and compared it to a real-life experiment involving a superconducting atom, showing that their predictions aligned with the data. By deciphering the underlying dynamics of these systems, they were able to map the relationship between their components, providing a graphical representation that could be used to forecast the particle's state in the Jaynes-Cummings model. In a broader context, this achievement demonstrates how graph neural networks can be used to analyze open quantum systems, offering a new perspective on the celebrated Heisenberg uncertainty principle. By understanding this principle's breakdown, researchers can identify the point at which complex quantum systems become unpredictable, and they have the potential to explore other unvisited areas of physics. The data and methods used in this study are available for public use. The code is based on a open-source neural network library called PyTorch, and the simulation and measurement data are in standardized formats. Knowledge Tracing (KT) models leverage student interaction data to predict intended knowledge, with evaluations typically assessing model performance on future actions. Despite their design, these models also demonstrate potential in forecasting specific past actions, which can be utilized for various purposes like identifying concept difficulties. Presently, knowledge tracing models are assessed using a forward-looking approach, focusing solely on subsequent interactions. In contrast, a backward-looking strategy considers previous data to evaluate model understanding. Our proposed Python framework, pyKT, facilitates both forward and backward-looking evaluations, allowing users to appraise knowledge tracing models from different perspectives. We demonstrate pyKT's capabilities by exploring a simple scenario where we assess model understanding by predicting past actions, revealing that models' ability to forecast earlier interactions varies significantly throughout a course. This finding's statistical significance is validated through a control experiment. Our findings highlight the value of examining models' ability to predict previous interactions, which can be discerned using the pyKT library. The pyKT library is available on GitHub at https://github.com/AmrElwahey/pyKT. The code for the control experiment is available at https://github.com/AmrElwahey/pyKT-Control-Experiment. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across different languages. This approach first trains a neural network on a related task then utilizes this trained model to accomplish the desired task. Neural network models have limited ability to ignore irrelevant information due to their widespread use, thereby making it challenging to ascertain that all learned features are relevant. To address this issue, a threshold is introduced to exclude irrelevant information, allowing for the selection of relevant features, which enhances the performance of subsequent tasks. This research involves developing a novel strategy that optimizes the neural network model to ignore irrelevant information, thereby further improving performance. A central approach and two alternative methods are presented to achieve this goal. The proposed central approach exploits the non-linear relationship between inputs and outputs, thereby reducing the number of features by 90%. The proposed research is applied to a speech recognition task where it delivers a 20% reduction in error rate compared to existing methods. Additionally, the system is tested for cross-language transferability, wherein it demonstrates a 10% reduction in error rate when transferred from a German dataset to an English dataset. Furthermore, the proposed method is compared to other baselines on a publicly available dataset, wherein it delivers a 15% reduction in error rate compared to the current state-of-the-art. The proposed research has the potential to be expanded to other tasks beyond speech recognition. Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges that robotic guides face when navigating through complex underwater environments. By merging Gaussian Process regression and TD learning, our method provides a way to make predictive statements about future rewards by utilizing sparse representations that significantly reduce computational requirements. Our algorithm's effectiveness was demonstrated in a simulated undersea scenario in which the guide navigates an air-filled bubble to reach a submerged target, and also in a real-world scenario where the guide navigates through a maze to reach a hidden treasure. Our results show that our approach outperforms existing methods across various assessment metrics. Our code is available at: https://github.com/AAinA/SparseGPTD.

We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a self-gravitating anisotropic relativistic star in terms of dual-fluid objects within General Relativity. The 1+1+2 covariant formalism allows for a clear and intuitive expression of the Einstein field equations in terms of semi-tetrad components. By making assumptions about the pressure and density relationships in the dual objects, we derive a set of nonlinear differential equations that the metric components must satisfy. Our method yields precise expressions for the metric components, which can be further used to investigate various aspects of the star, such as its boundary, horizon, and interior properties. Additionally, we establish a connection between our 1+1+2 covariant approach and previously established results obtained through other methods. Our analysis encompasses both static and dynamical configurations, and we provide specific solutions for particular pressure and density relationships. Furthermore, we demonstrate how our 1+1+2 covariant method can be applied to study the star's evolution and its interface properties. Our work offers a versatile non-linear 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad description of the star's dynamics and its interior properties, which can be utilized in various approximation schemes, such as perturbation theories, WKB approximations, and others. This research is relevant to astrophysical contexts involving self-gravitating rotating dwarf stars, as well as binary mergers and neutron star collisions. This work is also an extension of previous studies on the subject matter. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve model performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper leverages the meta-learning framework to achieve high-quality GEC results on novel domains with just a dozen labeled examples. We demonstrate that using few sample adaptations within the meta-learning process enhances the effectiveness of GEC models, with performance gains observed in both the domain adaptation and general GEC tasks. Our proposed approach achieves a superior result compared to baseline methods, surpassing the current state-of-the-art in domain-adaptation GEC tasks by a significant margin according to evaluation metrics. Moreover, the model's ability to generalize to new domains is so effective that it even surpasses the performance of models trained on a large, unified GEC dataset. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/ghrua/meta-gcc.

Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of hadron structure is performed by calculating the precise form of generalized parton distributions (GPDs) in the pion, across a wide range of momentum transfers. The analysis relies on two distinct methods, involving the expansion of a quasi-distribution integral in a expansion of two currents. The results from both approaches are compared, demonstrating consistency and valuing insight into the underlying theory. Moreover, the investigation delves into the implications of two-current correlations on GPDs, offering a nuanced understanding of their underlying components. The study further explores the connection between GPDs and quasi-distribution counterparts, providing numerical data that supplements earlier findings, especially in the realm of large momentum transfers. The lattice findings are also translated into physical units, facilitating a deeper comprehension of the internal mechanics of the pion. The study paves the way for expanding the analysis to other hadrons, with the pion serving as a testing ground, and offers a framework for extracting tangible information about partonic structure from lattice calculations. The numerical outcomes are made readily accessible for further use. The research presented has been previously published in the journal Physical Review Letters (Volume 128, Issue 4 - 2022) and Nuclear Physics B (Volume 994 - 2021). Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
robust and secure systems involving multiple interacting components.
However, offline learning struggles with diverse, potentially
malignant data featuring agents acting independently and collaboratively,
complicating the creation of universally trustworthy models.
We address this challenge by concentrating on the subset of collaborative
behaviors and developing a method called Collaborative Path Learning (CPL).
CPL selectively focuses on data involving interacting agents and extracts the
most beneficial paths, disregarding path credits.
We evaluate CPL against multiple baselines and comparable methods in scenarios
featuring complex collaborative behaviors in gaming environments and real-world
settings, including traffic scenarios generated by SUMO. Our findings indicate
CPL consistently outperforms the baselines across various assessment metrics. 
Our code is available at https://github.com/GroupMind-AI/CPL.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to create codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Furthermore, the method's applicability is demonstrated across FDD systems, including 5G NL-DPD transmitter scenarios. Feedback encoding and codebook creation-related overhead are analyzed, and the proposed approach shows significant advantages over traditional methods, such as TDD-based training and conventional FDD systems. Moreover, simulation results indicate that the GMM-based approach can be effective in various 5G scenarios, including massive MIMO systems. The code for this research is available online, providing further details about GMM-based codebook creation, feedback encoding, and associated simulations.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
To demonstrate its effectiveness, we utilized TextWorldExpress to conduct difficult tests of three leading text-based game challenges, uncovering performance gaps of up to twenty times when compared to traditional simulations. 
The express version is available online at textworldexpress.com.

We aim to investigate the importance of multiple research aspects, including the structure of models, data, and computation, and demonstrate the robustness of Bayes factors through a series of studies. Specifically, we examined the impact of different model configurations, tested a simple approach for validating models, explored various computation techniques for Bayesian estimation, and investigated the relationship between Bayes factor and other metrics such as Bayesian model selection, posterior probability, and posterior model probability. Our findings showed that Bayes factors are sensitive indicators that reflect the fit of a model to the observed data, and we provide practical guidelines for researchers to select appropriate models, validate research designs, and efficiently conduct Bayesian estimation. Ultimately, our work is intended to contribute to the accurate use of Bayes factors in cognitive science research. Discourse markers such as "however," play a significant role in connecting sentences and paragraphs, and their meaning can vary depending on their position within a text. Although numerous AI models, including language inference systems and generative models, have achieved high performance, they often falter when analyzing the semantic function of discourse markers. To address this shortcoming, we present DiscSense, a unique tool designed to automate the examination of discourse markers' semantic function in a given text. This entailing three main tasks: (1) identifying the discourse markers, (2) determining their semantic function, and ((3) analyzing the surrounding context. We employ a custom-made interface and command-line functionality to accomplish these objectives. Alongside this innovation, we establish a comprehensive dataset encompassing 7200 text segments to facilitate research and development in this area. Existing approaches fail to accurately assess the semantic function of discourse markers, offering room for improvement as demonstrated by our experiments. We envision DiscSense serving as a valuable platform for researchers and developers alike, providing a foundation for either standalone usage or integration into existing systems, as shown in our demo. The underlying code along with guidance on replication are available at https://github.com/ghrasoul/DiscSense. Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. After exploring existing methods that solely focus on accuracy enhancement, we present a new framework called Activation Range Supervision (ARS) to create a robust case for the safety of CNNs against hardware-induced memory malfunctions. The proposed ARS framework consists of three key components: initial training, range restriction, and dynamic thresholding. We tested ARS on MNIST, TNIST, and ResNet-18 and found it to be highly effective in protecting CNNs against hardware errors. In particular, ARS successfully prevented faulty memory-induced errors in 99.25% of cases on TNIST. Additionally, ARS demonstrated superior performance compared to alternative methods like robust optimization and adversarial training. The proposed framework provides a reliable safety guarantee without compromising efficiency, as shown by a 1.5x speedup of ResNet-18 on TNIST compared to a robust baseline. The results of our experiments are also reflected in the performance of ARS on more complex networks like RegNetY, ReLU-Net, and MobileNetV3. The proposed ARS framework offers a tangible means of constructing a robust case for the safety of CNNs against hardware-induced memory malfunctions. Our technique involves defining a directed graph, dividing multilingual word embeddings into distinct clusters while maintaining linguistic consistency, and applying the deepWalk algorithm to extract semantic features. We have tested our approach on four languages (English, French, Spanish, and Portuguese) and found that our method outperforms reference models in tasks such as monolingual sentiment analysis and binary change detection. Our method has a straightforward implementation requiring a limited number of parameters, making it a practical and efficient solution for interpreting high-dimensional word embeddings within clusters and across multiple languages. Mobile robots and autonomous systems require efficient and robust localization techniques. Despite the small size of visual-inertial sensors, their accuracy has been shown to surpass that of inertial measurement units (IMUs alone) in indoor environments. However, processing visual-inertial data consumes significant computational power. This paper presents a novel visual-inertial localization network, capable of balancing accuracy and efficiency. The proposed framework leverages external memory in attention networks to minimize computational overhead, even while operating at high frame rates. The model's ability to learn from supervised training allows it to be trained once, rather than requiring continuous optimization, resulting in a computationally efficient approach. The EMA-VIO network demonstrates superior performance when compared to state-of-the-art methods in various evaluation metrics, including precision, recall, and mean squared error. Moreover, its lightweight design facilitates seamless integration into various applications, as evidenced by its successful deployment on a tiny custom visual-inertial sensor board. The code for this research is available at this link https://github.com/yousef-ali/EMA-VIO.

A novel class of materials, dubbed "square-root Weyl" materials, is proposed, which incorporates a novel, more complex spinor function that can be applied to topological physics. These materials would have unique properties, such as zero-fold degeneracy and a constant Berry curvature, and researchers predict the existence of exotic quasiparticles, referred to as half-quantum vortices, which could be realized in experimentally accessible situations. A general framework for describing these materials has been established and applied to a specific scenario, involving square-root Weyl states in a 2D honeycomb lattice, which exhibits both chiral and orbital magnetism. This has enabled the prediction of one-way vortex streets along specific directions and the occurrence of mass-acceleration dichotomy. Additionally, it has been demonstrated that square-root Weyl materials can be engineered in a 3D cubic lattice, resulting in the creation of half-quantum vortex lines with net polarization and zero-fold degeneracy along specific directions. This represents a theoretical breakthrough in topological physics, with potential applications awaiting experimental verification.

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson postulated that the total Pontrjagin class of a manifold could be determined by local geometric data, specifically the orientation and normal bundle. We provide a derived aspect of their conjecture, rephrased using the language of singular chains. Additionally, we offer a straightforward proof of this revised statement. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the total Pontrjagin class can be computed using a simplified version of the original combinatorial formula proposed by Gelfand and MacPherson. The revised formula eliminates the need for the Borel equivariant cohomology of a point. The derived aspect of the conjecture has implications for the development of a theory of the total Pontrjagin class for infinite-dimensional manifolds constructed from finite-dimensional components. The application to such manifolds is demonstrated. The relationship between two variations of the combinatorial formula proposed by Gelfand and MacPherson is also explored. The paper concludes by examining the combinatorial formula in the context of an infinite-dimensional manifold given by an infinite set of geometric equations. The analysis reveals that the formula provides a meaningful answer for this type of manifold; however, the answer cannot be determined from the Borel equivariant cohomology of the space defined by the equations. The result offers insight into the difficulties of extending the development of the total Pontrjagin class from finite-dimensional manifolds to infinite-dimensional manifolds given by finite-dimensional components. The paper includes an appendix detailing the relationship between the Borel equivariant cohomology of a space and the cohomology of the space. The discussion provides background information for the problem under consideration and offers a blueprint for analyzing an infinite set of geometric equations. The analysis of the combinatorial formula also offers a way to determine the cohomology of the space defined by the equations, which can be used to solve the equations and thereby the manifold. The approach is demonstrated with an example. The example involves an infinite set of geometric equations with an infinite set of U(1)-actions on infinite-dimensional vector spaces. The example shows that the development of the total Pontrjagin class for manifolds given by U(1)-equations can be based on the development of the total Pontrjagin class for finite-dimensional manifolds. The relationship between the cohomology of the space defined by the equations and the Borel equivariant cohomology of the space is also demonstrated.

We investigated the photometric and spectroscopic characteristics of a rare Type II supernova called SN 2020jfo. This SN exhibited abnormally brief luminosity and dust formation periods, we found. Comparing its spectral features to those of other similar SNe, SN 2020jfo was initially similar, but its development slowed significantly. An exceptionally brief plateau phase is a hallmark of SNe with high mass loss rates, yet this isn't usually combined with other characteristics of this type, such as weak hydrogen lines and extensive [Ni II] absorption. This unusual combination may indicate that SN 2020jfo resulted from a 12 solar mass star with substantial mass loss, rather than the 8 to 16 solar masses typically associated with this type of SN. Furthermore, the absence of massive star indicators in SN 2020jfo's spectra is also consistent with this analysis. This study was collaborative with the OGLE and the ASAS-SN collaboration.

The detection of X-rays in wide-field observations poses a challenge due to the limited field of vision of most X-ray detectors. A typical detector can only observe a small portion of the sky at any given time, leaving a large area for further investigation. To address this issue, we propose an innovative arrangement featuring a lobster-eye (LE) optic configuration consisting of multiple, independently positioned LE units. Each LE unit has its own CMOS camera, allowing for simultaneous area coverage and enhanced event localization. This optic arrangement can be optimally designed to maximize the monitored area while maintaining a high degree of sensitivity, and we provide an example design for a 4-unit LE arrangement that could potentially cover over 2 square degrees with a 5.3 micron pixel size, and feature a 30 arcminute field of view for each unit. This concept has been applied to a design that could be suitable for the eROSITA X-ray telescope, and further research is needed to fully evaluate this idea. This proposed LE arrangement presents a novel approach to X-ray detection that could also be adapted for other types of electromagnetic radiation.
